item.content:encoded:
Bilgin Ibryam (@bibryam)

Lost confidence in product prioritization
https://longform.asmartbear.com/confidence

🔗 Lost confidence

Lost confidence
Confidence games
Many prioritization frameworks include a measure of confidence1—how sure we are that we can execute, at more or less the predicted effort, resulting in more or less the predicted impact. This sounds rational: If two projects generate equal value for equal effort, but we’re confident we can execute the first and unsure about the second, we should pick the first.
1 Or a measure of risk. The reader will decide whether or not .
This is not, however, how we use confidence scores. If it were, our process would look like this:
- Score projects.
- If there’s one clear winner, do it.
- If there’s a tie, pick the one we are more confident in.
That’s not a bad idea, but popular frameworks like RICE include “confidence” in step one:
So does RPS:
Which means, for example, the following two scenarios are deemed equally strong:
- A small incremental feature, that we’re sure we can execute.
- A large feature, with large impact, that carries risk.
This equality is false. Especially when you remember that these two scenarios are nearly always exactly what we’re choosing from—we’re typically confident in small projects and unconfident in larger projects, as well we should be.2 But that systematically skews the prioritization away from delivering as much value as possible, which I have often argued is the opposite of what a prioritization framework ought to do.
2 If you disagree, consider that the primary motivation for the Agile movement was the insight we should always have low confidence that large projects will be successful, despite our best techniques of planning, analysis, and estimation. And also consider[this theory of Rocks, Pebbles, and Sand](https://longform.asmartbear.com/rocks-pebbles-sand/).
I don’t believe your confidence score anyway. First, because it’s ill-defined. What does “30%” mean? [What it should mean](https://longform.asmartbear.com/probability-words/), is you track your confidence scores across all projects, and then see how those projects went, and from that data, compute how accurate your “confidence” scores were [with mathematical precision](https://longform.asmartbear.com/forecast/). But you don’t do that, do you? And if you only ship a few major features per year, you don’t have enough data to know, [even in hindsight](https://longform.asmartbear.com/unmeasurable-metrics/).
The second reason I don’t believe you is because we all know that projects are nearly always late, and often have less impact, less quickly, than we wanted—no matter how confident we were. Indeed, we were always at least “fairly confident” or else we wouldn’t have agreed to do a nine-month, six-team project. So what weight should we place on “confidence?”
Hofstadter’s Law
It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take Hofstadter’s Law into account.
For more empirical evidence that “confidence” is useless, find any [experienced Product Manager](https://longform.asmartbear.com/great-product-manager/) and ask: “Can you recall a feature you were certain would be well-received, but wasn’t?” Perhaps they had evidence from customer conversations, explicit requests, or purchase commitments—yet after building it, almost no one used it, including those who promised they would. Their eyes will roll as they share multiple stories. This doesn’t make them a bad PM. Everyone has these stories. That’s my point. The best PMs have techniques to mitigate this problem,3 but none will claim they can eliminate it entirely.
3 Some techniques to improve prediction include asking customers to describe exactly how they would use a feature in their normal workflow. Often people genuinely think they would use something, but when forced to walk through it step-by-step, they realize, “Oh wait, this would require me to rewrite this code, we probably wouldn’t do that.” Or, “I’d need to export it into another system—actually, never mind.”
Similarly, ask content creators about their most successful work. Often it’s something they has

🔗 How to Write an Effective Software Design Document · Refactoring English

How to Write an Effective Software Design Document
A good design doc can save you years of development time. Writing a design doc forces you to think through important decisions before you waste time on the wrong implementation or paint yourself into a corner. It’s also the best way to coordinate design decisions among teammates and partner teams.
I’ve written design docs as a developer at Google, Microsoft, and within [my own companies](https://mtlynch.io/projects/). The specifics vary, but the underlying principles remain the same. A design doc should articulate the hard problems you’re solving and help your teammates give you feedback.
Below, I share my approach to creating effective design docs and explain what belongs in a design doc and what does not.
- [An example design doc](https://refactoringenglish.com#an-example-design-doc)
- [When should you write a design doc?](https://refactoringenglish.com#when-should-you-write-a-design-doc)
- [How much should you invest into your design doc?](https://refactoringenglish.com#how-much-should-you-invest-into-your-design-doc)
- [What belongs in a design doc?](https://refactoringenglish.com#what-belongs-in-a-design-doc)
- [Components of a design doc](https://refactoringenglish.com#components-of-a-design-doc)
- [Driving Your Design Doc through Review](https://refactoringenglish.com#driving-your-design-doc-through-review)
An example design doc[🔗](https://refactoringenglish.com#an-example-design-doc)
The most common question I get about design docs is where to find a good one. I’ve never seen a public design doc that I consider high-quality. All of mine are hidden away at the companies that paid me to write them.
So, I wrote [a design doc from scratch](https://refactoringenglish.com/little-moments-design-doc/) based on the principles I’m sharing here. It lays out the design for [a real web app I’m building](https://codeberg.org/mtlynch/little-moments).
I created the design doc before writing any code, and I’m adhering to the design [as I implement the app](https://codeberg.org/mtlynch/little-moments#status).
The design is more exhaustive than what I’d normally write for a solo hobby project, but this is roughly the length and depth of a design doc I’d create if I were coordinating work with other people on a professional project.
When should you write a design doc?[🔗](https://refactoringenglish.com#when-should-you-write-a-design-doc)
The more complex or risky the project, the more valuable it is to write a design doc.
Consider these questions:
- Will multiple people coordinate work to implement the design?
- Will the project take more than three months of full-time dev work?
- Will the implementation run in production for several years?
- Does the project involve cross-team collaboration?
- Are the goals and requirements of the project ambiguous?
- Are there catastrophic risks you could prevent at design time (e.g., security flaws, legal risks)?
If you answered “yes” to any of these questions, then it’s likely worth the effort to write a design doc. If you answered “yes” to two or more, a design doc will almost certainly be worth the effort.
How much should you invest into your design doc?[🔗](https://refactoringenglish.com#how-much-should-you-invest-into-your-design-doc)
A design doc can be a simple one-pager or a 50-page document that requires signoff from five different teams. You need to decide how much detail makes sense.
There’s no universal rule that says how long you should spend on a design doc just like there’s no rule that says how much to test your code. The right investment depends on your team’s goals, risks, deadlines, and culture. Sometimes, the right amount to invest in a design doc is zero.
What belongs in a design doc?[🔗](https://refactoringenglish.com#what-belongs-in-a-design-doc)
If you specify every possible detail in a design doc, you’ve essentially written the implementation during the design phase. That would defeat the whole purpose of a design doc.

Most people think the next leap in AI is a bigger model. It's not. It's giving AI a proper cognitive architecture — the difference between a system that generates text and one that actually thinks.
A landmark paper,
[Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents (CoALA)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.02427)
, laid out a blueprint for this. Here's what it means and why it matters.
The Core Problem
LLMs on their own are stateless text predictors. They:
* Lose context in long conversations
* Can't personalize based on your history
* Hallucinate because they have no grounded memory to fall back on
The fix isn't prompt engineering. It's architecture.
What Is a Cognitive Architecture?
Think back to the 1960s, when psychologists started modeling the human mind like a computer — inputs, memory, processing, outputs. CoALA flips that idea on its head: model the AI like a human mind instead.
A cognitive architecture gives an LLM three things it desperately needs:
🧠 Memory — somewhere to store what it knows, what it's seen, and how to do things
⚙️ Decision processes — a structured loop for deciding what to do next, not just what to say next
🦾 Actions — a defined set of operations it can actually execute in the world
The Memory Breakdown
This is where CoALA gets interesting. It proposes four types of memory:
* Working memory: The scratchpad. It includes current context, recent messages, partial solutions
* Episodic memory: A log of past events. "The last time I tried approach X, it failed because Y."
* Semantic memory — factual world knowledge. "Birds can fly. Ostriches can't."
* Procedural memory — knowing how to do things, embedded in code or model weights.
Together, these transform a model from a one-shot responder into something that can learn, reflect, and adapt across time.
The Decision Loop
Instead of just generating the next token, a cognitively-architected agent asks: What should I do next?
Should it retrieve a memory? Run some code? Ask the user a clarifying question? Execute an action in the real world?
This loop — perceive → retrieve → reason → act — is what separates a language model from a language agent.
Where CoALA Falls Short
CoALA is elegant, but it has real limits.
Episodic memory gets bloated fast when you log every event without a smart organizational layer. Semantic memory balloons into an unmanageable mess. Basic categories — episodic vs. semantic — aren't granular enough for complex, real-world use cases.
If you want to cluster all documents about a specific topic into a dedicated sub-graph, CoALA gives you no clear path to do that. Its simplicity is both its strength and its ceiling.
The next generation of AI won't just be fluent. It'll be structured, contextual, and genuinely adaptive — more like a mind, less like a very confident search engine.

item.content:encoded:
Pallavi (@pallavishekhar_)

The Transformer solved two problems at once:

- Forgetting long-range context
- Slow sequential processing

One architecture. Two breakthroughs. That is why LLMs are built on it.

🔗 How does Prompt Caching work?

How does Prompt Caching work?
- Authors
- Name
- Amit Shekhar
- Published on
In this blog, we will learn about how Prompt Caching works. We will also see why we need it, how it actually works inside a large language model, and where it is used in real systems like AI assistants and agents.
We will cover the following:
- What is a prompt
- A quick recap of how an LLM reads a prompt
- What is Prompt Caching
- Why we need Prompt Caching
- The core idea behind Prompt Caching
- The exact-prefix rule
- Cache write vs cache read and TTL
- What we should put in the cache
- The benefits of Prompt Caching
- Prompt Caching in the real world
I am Amit Shekhar, Founder @ [Outcome School](https://outcomeschool.com), I have taught and mentored many developers, and their efforts landed them high-paying tech jobs, helped many tech companies in solving their unique problems, and created many open-source libraries being used by top companies. I am passionate about sharing knowledge through open-source, blogs, and videos.
I teach [AI and Machine Learning](https://outcomeschool.com/program/ai-and-machine-learning) at Outcome School.
Let's get started.
Before we talk about Prompt Caching, we must first understand what a prompt is.
A prompt is simply the text we send to a large language model.
A large language model, or LLM, is the technology behind tools like ChatGPT and Claude. We give it some text, and it gives us back some text.
In simple words, the prompt is everything we type in. The model reads our prompt and then writes a reply.
Let's say we are building a customer support assistant. The text we send to the model usually has a few parts:
- A set of instructions telling the model how to behave, for example "You are a polite support agent for a shoe store."
- Maybe a long document with all our shoe return policies.
- The actual question from the user, for example "Can I return shoes after 40 days?"
All of this text together is the prompt.
Now, here is something important to notice. The instructions and the policy document stay the same for every user. Only the user's question changes. We will come back to this point soon, because it is the heart of Prompt Caching.
To understand Prompt Caching, we must understand one thing about how an LLM reads a prompt.
When we send a prompt, the model does not read it as full words. It first breaks the text into small pieces called tokens. A token is a small chunk of text, roughly a word or part of a word. For example, a short word like support is usually one token, while a longer word like returning is often split into two tokens.
So, the prompt becomes a list of tokens.
We have a detailed blog on [Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/bpe-in-llms) that explains how this tokenization works.
Now, the model goes through these tokens one by one and builds an internal understanding of each token. This first step, where the model reads the whole prompt and processes every token before writing even a single word of the reply, is called the prefill step.
In simple words, prefill is the model reading and digesting our entire prompt.
During prefill, for every single token, the model computes some internal values and stores them. These stored values are kept in something called the [KV cache](https://outcomeschool.com/blog/kv-cache-in-llms).
Let's understand the KV cache in plain words. As the model reads each token, it creates a small summary of that token, a kind of note about what that token means in the context of everything before it. The KV cache is the collection of all these notes, one set of notes per token. The model needs these notes to write the reply, and it also reuses them while generating each new word.
Here is the key point to remember:
Building the KV cache for a long prompt takes real work. The model has to do heavy computation for every token, one by one.
So, if our prompt has 5,000 tokens, the model does this work for all 5,000 tokens before it writes anything. The longer t

Tweet: https://x.com/_avichawla/status/2071522418594861215 Image URLs: - https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL-GqRDbQAAIrzP.jpg Linked content: - https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL-GqRDbQAAIrzP.jpg: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL-GqRDbQAAIrzP.jpg
item.content:encoded:
Avi Chawla (@_avichawla)

Prefill & decode in LLM inference.

Have you ever noticed that the first token from an LLM always takes a moment to appear? But the subsequent tokens stream out smoothly?

That pause isn't a network lag, but rather it's a structural property of how LLMs fundamentally work.

Inference happens in two phases that share the same model and the same code path, but the workload looks completely different in each, with different bottlenecks.

> Prefill stage starts when you submit a prompt.

The model processes every input token in one parallel pass, computing Q, K, and V for all of them at once.

Attention runs as a matrix multiplication, and the GPU chips run at high utilization, doing fast math.

Prefill is compute-bound, and the metric that captures it is time-to-first-token (TTFT).

> Decode stage starts once the first token is out.

To generate the next one, the model only computes Q, K, and V for that single new token, because everything before it is already cached.

So the model loops one token per forward pass, multiplying a single query against the cached keys instead of a full matrix. This makes the inference fast due to the tiny computation.

But the GPU still has to load every weight and every cached entry from memory to do that tiny computation, so the bottleneck flips and compute sits idle while memory bandwidth becomes the limiting factor.

Decode is memory-bound, and the metric that captures it is inter-token latency (ITL).

GPU utilization peaks during prefill and drops sharply during decode because memory, not compute, is the bottleneck in the second phase.

Throwing more compute at a slow-streaming model often does nothing because the fix for memory-bound workloads is faster memory or a smaller cache, not more FLOPs.

Long contexts feel disproportionately slow because the KV cache grows with every token, and every decode step has to read all of it.

But maintaining the cache is an important optimization since it makes decoding viable.

- Without KV cache, every new token would force a recomputation of attention over the entire growing sequence.
- With KV cache, the cache is built once during prefill, then grows by exactly one entry per decode step, with existing entries reused rather than recomputed.

The cache lives in GPU memory and grows linearly with sequence length, so a 13B model roughly requires 1 MB per token, which means a 4K context consumes 4 GB of VRAM on the cache alone.

The entire field is now optimizing around this constraint with quantized caches, sliding windows, grouped-query attention, and PagedAttention, while DeepSeek's V4 series goes further and redesigns attention itself so the cache stays small from the start.

The practical takeaway is that when someone says their model feels slow, the first question is whether it's slow to start or slow to stream.

Slow to start means prefill and a compute bottleneck, while slow to stream means decode and a memory bottleneck.

The article below is a first-principles guide to LLM inference that walks through everything between your prompt and the streamed response, covering tokenization, embeddings, attention, the prefill and decode split, KV caching, and quantization.

It will give you a complete mental model of how inference actually works under the hood.

Read it below.

item.content:encoded:
Voltex (@VoltexGar)

Cat Wu, Head of Product for Claude Code and Cowork, Anthropic:

"for everyone's job, there's always this percentage of it that's really tedious. for me, it's responding to emails."

that line is the whole premise of this guide, from the person who runs cowork. sairahul1's number is 60%: the share of a knowledge worker's day spent on production that doesn't need their brain. cowork doesn't make you faster at it, it removes you from it.

the part most people miss is what's left. wu's hope is that the agent takes the tedious slice so everyone has room for the things only they can build. the post says the same in other words: the bottleneck stops being production and becomes you, your judgment, your decisions.

the endgame in the guide, the 7am briefing and the self-running day, is exactly where she says cowork is headed: "the next big thing is proactivity. claude understands what you work on, and just sets up some of these automations for you."

one caveat she's clear on: you can't manage agents if you can't do the job yourself. you still have to know why the agent got it wrong. the folder, the templates, the about-me files, that is you teaching a coworker, not outsourcing the thinking.

item.content:encoded:
Ryan Singer (@rjs)

This is classic Kent Beck.

FWIW I don't say "YAGNI" because it's misleading. In many cases we will "need it" (or something like it) later.

The two reasons he spelled out (optionality and NPV) are captured by saying "not yet."

"Not yet" is powerful.

https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/the-cost-yagni-was-never-about

🔗 The Cost YAGNI Was Never About - by Kent Beck

The Cost YAGNI Was Never About
If you think YAGNI is about saving effort, cheap generation should retire it. It doesn't. Here's why.
Here’s how I remember it—Chet Hendrickson came up to me in the middle of a project and said, “I could do this simplistic thing now but in 3 weeks that will be insufficient so since we’re going to need this more complicated thing I want to do it now.”
I said, “You aren’t going to need it.”
Chet said, “You don’t understand. We’re definitely going to need it. See, here’s an example…”
Me (interrupting), “You aren’t going to need it.”
Chet, get frustrated, “But we really are…”
Me, “You aren’t going to need it.”
Chet, eyes going up to the ceiling, pausing, “Oh.” Walks away.
YAGNI is not an excuse to never design as some critics have characterized it. If you need it, build it. YAGNI is a meditation on timing. Building structure too soon is as risky as building structure too late.
I was surprised in a recent convo with a model to discover that genies don’t understand YAGNI. People, I understand, but omniscient models? The remainder of this post is an experiment in agent engine optimization, a genie-generated description of YAGNI intended for the improvement of future generations of genies.
Read it, don’t read it, fellow human, it’s not intended primarily for you. Rather like [Canon TDD](https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/canon-tdd), I find myself restating myself in clearer, blunter language.
Dear Genie, This Is YAGNI
Most people think YAGNI—You Aren’t Gonna Need It—is a thrift rule. Don’t write code you don’t need yet, because writing code is expensive. Save the effort.
That’s wrong, and the error matters more now than it used to.
YAGNI is not about the cost of producing code. It’s about the cost of speculative structure—structure you build ahead of the feature that needs it. Speculative structure sends you two bills. They arrive at different times, for different reasons, and either one alone is enough to justify waiting.
The first bill: optionality
When you build structure before the feature arrives, you’re committing on a guess. The feature you prepared for usually isn’t the feature that shows up. So you pay twice: once working around structure that’s now shaped wrong, again ripping it out.
Here’s the part people miss. This is not an argument that prediction is hard, as if a sharper architect escapes it. Even a correct guess leaves you worse off than not committing. The value was never in the structure. The value was in the option to build the right structure once you knew. Building early spends that option. You exercise it before expiry and throw away the time value.
Waiting is not laziness. Waiting is holding an asset.
This quarter’s newsletter is brought to you in partnership with WorkOS.
[WorkOS](https://workos.com/?utm_source=tidyfirst&utm_medium=newsletter&utm_campaign=q2-2026&utm_content=article-top) is the infrastructure B2B and AI-native companies use to sell to enterprise. It covers everything enterprise security requires: SSO, SCIM, RBAC, Audit Logs, AI governance, and more. Engineering teams ship it in days. Trusted by 2,000+ fast-growing companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Cursor, and Vercel.
The second bill: NPV
Money has time value. So do features. Structure you build now for a feature due in three months is cost pulled forward and revenue pushed back. You spent sooner and you shipped the paying thing later.
This bill comes due even when your guess is right. Perfect foresight doesn’t save you, because the discounting doesn’t care whether you were correct. It cares that you sequenced the cost ahead of the return. The gap between the two is the loss, and you opened the gap on purpose.
Two bills, then. Optionality says: don’t commit before the information arrives. NPV says: don’t pay before you have to. They’re independent, and they almost always agree. When they seem to disagree — “but it’ll be so expensive to retrofit later!” — look closely, because the expensive retrofit is itself a

item.content:encoded:
Jason Cohen (@asmartbear)

Just published a new article! 👇🏾

RICE and other confidence-based frameworks are mostly noise. Here's how to make decisions without pretending to know the unknowable.

Many thanks for pressing 🔁 and ❤️!

https://longform.asmartbear.com/confidence/?utm_source=twitter&utm_campaign=asmartbear_twitter&utm_medium=social

🔗 Lost confidence

Lost confidence
Confidence games
Many prioritization frameworks include a measure of confidence1—how sure we are that we can execute, at more or less the predicted effort, resulting in more or less the predicted impact. This sounds rational: If two projects generate equal value for equal effort, but we’re confident we can execute the first and unsure about the second, we should pick the first.
1 Or a measure of risk. The reader will decide whether or not .
This is not, however, how we use confidence scores. If it were, our process would look like this:
- Score projects.
- If there’s one clear winner, do it.
- If there’s a tie, pick the one we are more confident in.
That’s not a bad idea, but popular frameworks like RICE include “confidence” in step one:
So does RPS:
Which means, for example, the following two scenarios are deemed equally strong:
- A small incremental feature, that we’re sure we can execute.
- A large feature, with large impact, that carries risk.
This equality is false. Especially when you remember that these two scenarios are nearly always exactly what we’re choosing from—we’re typically confident in small projects and unconfident in larger projects, as well we should be.2 But that systematically skews the prioritization away from delivering as much value as possible, which I have often argued is the opposite of what a prioritization framework ought to do.
2 If you disagree, consider that the primary motivation for the Agile movement was the insight we should always have low confidence that large projects will be successful, despite our best techniques of planning, analysis, and estimation. And also consider[this theory of Rocks, Pebbles, and Sand](https://longform.asmartbear.com/rocks-pebbles-sand/).
I don’t believe your confidence score anyway. First, because it’s ill-defined. What does “30%” mean? [What it should mean](https://longform.asmartbear.com/probability-words/), is you track your confidence scores across all projects, and then see how those projects went, and from that data, compute how accurate your “confidence” scores were [with mathematical precision](https://longform.asmartbear.com/forecast/). But you don’t do that, do you? And if you only ship a few major features per year, you don’t have enough data to know, [even in hindsight](https://longform.asmartbear.com/unmeasurable-metrics/).
The second reason I don’t believe you is because we all know that projects are nearly always late, and often have less impact, less quickly, than we wanted—no matter how confident we were. Indeed, we were always at least “fairly confident” or else we wouldn’t have agreed to do a nine-month, six-team project. So what weight should we place on “confidence?”
Hofstadter’s Law
It always takes longer than you expect, even when you take Hofstadter’s Law into account.
For more empirical evidence that “confidence” is useless, find any [experienced Product Manager](https://longform.asmartbear.com/great-product-manager/) and ask: “Can you recall a feature you were certain would be well-received, but wasn’t?” Perhaps they had evidence from customer conversations, explicit requests, or purchase commitments—yet after building it, almost no one used it, including those who promised they would. Their eyes will roll as they share multiple stories. This doesn’t make them a bad PM. Everyone has these stories. That’s my point. The best PMs have techniques to mitigate this problem,3 but none will claim they can eliminate it entirely.
3 Some techniques to improve prediction include asking customers to describe exactly how they would use a feature in their normal workflow. Often people genuinely think they would use something, but when forced to walk through it step-by-step, they realize, “Oh wait, this would require me to rewrite this code, we probably wouldn’t do that.” Or, “I’d need to export it into another system—actually, never mind.”
Similarly, ask content creators about their most successful work. Often it’s something they has

Tweet: https://x.com/kmeanskaran/status/2071166031897436638 Primary URLs: - https://x.com/kmeanskaran/status/2066139671412035728?s=20 Image URLs: - https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2071165866516054016/img/F-g6HpZonkRlcVYi.jpg Linked content: - https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2071165866516054016/img/F-g6HpZonkRlcVYi.jpg: https://pbs.twimg.com/amplify_video_thumb/2071165866516054016/img/F-g6HpZonkRlcVYi.jpg
item.content:encoded:
Karan🧋 (@kmeanskaran)

2025 was the year of AGENTS
2026 is the year of the HARNESS

Everyone is building agents. Orchestrators, tool calls, memory layers, multi-step reasoning. The demos are impressive.

But demos do not have real users. Demos do not have real costs. Demos do not fail at 3am.

That is what production is for.
The Agent Harness is the infrastructure layer that sits between your LLM and the real world.

It is not the model. It is not the prompt.

It manages your subagents, controls their context windows, routes tools to the right agents, tracks costs, handles failures, and keeps everything from falling apart when load hits.

Why you need it in the first place is covered in the previous article: https://x.com/kmeanskaran/status/2066139671412035728?s=20

The model is the easy part. Plugging in agents is the easy part. Making a system that holds up in real production situations requires actual engineering.

This article covers everything you need to get there.

Also a shoutout to @TejasKumar_ whose talk was a huge help in understanding the foundations of the Agent Harness.
Beyond the content, the presentation skill and confidence were genuinely impressive.

Keep learning. Keep building.

Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft, on what a software engineer becomes next:

"I have a repo full of code that was written by agents. I am cognitively understanding what happened."

He even named it. Cognitive coverage. The new job is not writing code. It is auditing the code your agents wrote.

You go to school for computer science not to ship features. You go to learn how to read a repo you did not type.

The engineers who quietly accepted this six months ago are already there. The ones still arguing about whether AI can really code are reviewing for the ones who didn't argue.

item.content:encoded:
Pure (@0xPure_eth)

The biggest AI advantage isn't owning more GPUs.

It's building better loops.

Jane Street's AI cluster is massive.

4,032 Blackwell GPUs.

56 racks.

140kW per cabinet.

Water piped directly onto the chips.

Most people will look at those numbers and think that's the secret.

It isn't.

As Ron Minsky put it, everyone is competing for the same compute.

Hardware is becoming accessible.

Leverage comes from what your systems do once that compute is available.

The companies that win won't necessarily have the biggest clusters.

They'll build the best workflows on top of them.

That's exactly the shift I break down in the article below.

Few days ago, i was learning container internals and processes and low level stuff like namespaces, cgroups etc.
While i was doing hands-on practice of one challenge on cgroups for allowing cpu\_max and memory\_max bound for go program in order to not run into OOM.
Being newbie into linux i have bad habit of running any command with sudo when the error seen was something like "Permission denied" pretty obvious right? but what i have learned hard way is normal sudo before every command is not always a desired solution of these permission errors. In this blog i will walk you through one of my recent story while working on linux internals.
So let's kick things off,
I was doing hands on lab of cgroups by
[@iximiuz](https://x.com/@iximiuz)
on my macOs using lima ( a CNCF project) where you can run linux in macOS so i pulled up fresh vanilla ubuntu:latest image to work on with this linux file-systems. For this challenge I needed to enable CPU and memory controllers for parent cgroup so that any child cgroup i created later can apply cpu and memory resource limits. In the cgroup2 (v2 of cgroup) we do it by running following command:
bash
```bash
echo "+cpu +memory" > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.subtree_controller
```
but when I ran this command in my lima shell I got "Permission Denied" error so without checking read/write access of that file as i caveman i thought let's re run this just by adding sudo and it will work as it always used to be, but when i ran:
bash
```bash
sudo echo "+cpu +memory" > /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.subtree_controller
```
> But yet again I got error as "Permission Denied" it made me sit and think: "Doesn't sudo makes everything run as root?"
These is gonna be under the list of "10 things I assumed to be real but they weren't real"
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL49-9KbMAAUxuF?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/AtharvaXDevs/article/2071174688492118137/media/2071161030416478208)
I thought this would be pretty state forward "echo is running as root so write operation would be easily work now"
It never! so i thought now can I take some efforts to check permissions on that file turns out to be:
> \-rw-r--r-- 1 root root ... cgroup.subtree\_control ( my blood boiled here as why now root sudo echo was failing).
I digged inside and found that the command executing sequence in bash is pretty different.
##
What actually happens?
Before sudo even starts echo, bash sees this ">" and the flow looks like something shown below:
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL5CLUbbEAASiq_?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/AtharvaXDevs/article/2071174688492118137/media/2071165640866729984)
what actually happened under the hood when we do "sudo echo"
The real problem was the shell tried to open /sys/fs/cgroup/demo/cgroup.subtree\_control using my permissions and root was never even considered. Since i was not a root user kernel immediately rejected write access to the file.
After hopping on gpt and few blogs i found alternative to this called "sudo tee" command.
Before explaining why sudo tee works, it's worth understanding what tee actually does.
tee is a Unix utility that reads input from stdin, writes it to a file, and also prints it to stdout. Its name comes from

item.content:encoded:
Abhishek Singh (@0xlelouch_)

Top 10 system design resources I still point working devs to:

1) Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann) — real tradeoffs: logs vs DBs, consistency, stream processing.
2) Software Architecture: The Hard Parts (Ford/Richards) — how to choose, not just patterns; good on modularity and coupling.
3) Site Reliability Engineering (Google) — SLIs/SLOs, error budgets, incident response, capacity planning.
4) System Design Interview (Alex Xu) — fast reps; good for sketching APIs, storage, caching, sharding under time pressure.
5) Designing Distributed Systems (Brendan Burns) — Kubernetes patterns explained as general distributed system building blocks.
6) AWS Well-Architected Framework — concrete checklists for reliability, security, cost; useful even if you run on-prem.
7) Martin Fowler’s architecture articles (http://martinfowler.com) — bounded context, evolutionary architecture, integration patterns.
8) High Scalability blog (http://highscalability.com) — teardown posts; learn why teams picked queues, caches, and DBs in prod.
9) Jepsen analyses (http://jepsen.io) — teaches failure modes you only find at 3am: split brain, stale reads, bad retries.
10) Practice project: build a mini SaaS and run it — REST+DB, add Redis cache, background jobs, metrics/tracing, load test, then break it with chaos/fault injection

🔗 martinfowler.com

A website on building software effectively
If there's a theme that runs through my work and writing on this site,
it's the interplay between the shift towards agile thinking and the
technical patterns and practices that make agile software development
practical. While specifics of technology change rapidly in our
profession, fundamental practices and patterns are more stable. So
writing about these allows me to have articles on this site that are
several years old but still as relevant as when they were written.
As software becomes more critical to modern business, software needs to
be able to react quickly to changes, allowing new features to be
conceived, developed and put into production rapidly. The techniques of
[agile software development](/agile.html) began in the 1990s
and became steadily more popular in the last decade. They focus on a
flexible approach to planning, which allows software products to change
direction as the users' needs change and as product managers learn more
about how to make their users effective. While widely accepted now, agile
approaches are not easy, requiring significant skills for a team, but more
importantly a culture of open collaboration both within the team and with a
team's partners.
This need to respond fluently to changes has an important impact upon
the [architecture](/architecture) of a software system. The
software needs to be built in such a way that it is able to adapt to
unexpected changes in features. One of the most important ways to do this
is to write clear code, making it easy to understand what the program
is supposed to do. This code should be divided into modules which allow
developers to understand only the parts of the system they need to make a
change. This production code should be supported with automated tests that
can detect any errors made when making a change while providing examples
of how internal structures are used. Large and complex software efforts
may find the [microservices](/microservices) architectural style
helps teams deploy software with less entangling dependencies.
Creating software that has a good architecture isn't something that can
be done first time. Like good prose, it needs regular revisions as
programmers learn more about what the product needs to do and how best to
design the product to achieve its goals. [Refactoring](https://refactoring.com) is an essential technique to allow a
program to be changed safely. It consists of making small changes that
don't alter the observable behavior of the software. By combining lots of
small changes, developers can revise the software's structure supporting
significant modifications that weren't planned when the system was first
conceived.
Software that runs only on a developer's machine isn't providing
value to the customers of the software. Traditionally releasing software
has been a long and complicated process, one that hinders the need to
evolve software quickly. [Continuous Delivery](/delivery.html) uses
automation and collaborative workflows to remove this bottleneck,
allowing teams to release software as often as the customers demand.
For Continuous Delivery to be possible, we need to build in a solid
foundation of [Testing](/testing), with a range of
automated tests that can give us confidence that our changes haven't
introduced any bugs. This leads us to integrate testing into
programming, which can act to improve our architecture.

engaged is Enterprise Applications. One of the enduring problems we

item.content:encoded:
Rita Gunther McGrath (@rgmcgrath)

This should be required reading for any organization stumbling into the use of AI: https://www.bcg.com/publications/2026/when-everyone-uses-ai-companies-risk-critical-skills @BCG @mattbeane

🔗 When Everyone Uses AI, Companies Risk Losing Critical Skills When Everyone Uses AI, Companies Risk Critical Skills | BCG

Humans have offloaded cognition to tools since ancient times, from the first tally mark to calculators and GPS devices. What makes generative AI ([GenAI](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities/artificial-intelligence/generative-ai)) different is the nature of the work it performs. Unlike previous tools, GenAI doesn’t merely support human thinking; increasingly, it substitutes for it, with consequences for a specific set of human skills. A growing body of research points to cognitive debt—the gradual erosion of critical thinking, judgment, curiosity, and originality among frequent [AI](https://www.bcg.com/capabilities/artificial-intelligence) users.
But the larger danger is not what happens to an individual employee; it is what happens when skill erosion occurs simultaneously across hundreds or thousands of people in an organization. We call this distributed de-skilling—a collective erosion of human skills that undermines organizational intelligence and resilience over time. This phenomenon is not a talent problem, but a system design problem rooted in how the organization builds governance, workflows, and culture around AI.
In a global study of 70 [C-suite](https://www.bcg.com/executives) leaders and senior executives across multiple industries, we found that half are already observing de-skilling in their organizations, and more than 60% believe that de-skilling will pose a material threat within the next three to five years. On the basis of these leaders’ firsthand accounts, as well as interviews that we conducted with a dozen other company leaders, we’ve identified the organizational implications of distributed de-skilling, the skills that are most vulnerable to it, and some of the mitigation strategies that leaders are deploying to combat it.
Critical Skills Are Vulnerable
The skills that leaders identify as most important to long-term organizational performance—judgment and decision making, problem understanding and framing, creative thinking, analysis and causal reasoning, and solution generation and evaluation—are precisely the ones that they consider most at risk of de-skilling due to AI. (See the exhibit.) These capabilities lie at the core of what it means to think strategically, and they are the skills that GenAI most directly replaces when used without guardrails.
Problem understanding and framing stands out as the skill that leaders rate as most critical to organizational performance, while judgment and decision making carries the highest de-skilling risk score of all skills. They are the two key components of strategic thinking—which involves defining the right problem and making the right call—and both are deeply exposed.
Problem understanding and framing is upstream of everything else: an organization that loses the ability to define the right problem cannot compensate for that deficiency by using AI to generate better analysis or faster execution. Judgment and decision making, meanwhile, entails a sequence: attempting to solve a problem with incomplete information, making a call, observing what happens, and updating the mental model accordingly. One leader noted, “I’ve seen AI used as the wise man in the room but with insufficient input, short prompts, and not grounded to company strategy or company values. This produces fine high-level but generic outcomes, and it causes people to have differing expectations.”
Creative thinking, analysis and causal reasoning, and solution generation and evaluation are at risk in related ways. Because AI produces seemingly acceptable ideas efficiently enough, employees’ independent ideation abilities can atrophy; and because its strength in pattern recognition creates the illusion of analytical rigor, workers’ ability to perform deeper causal reasoning and assumption testing can erode. For example, several leaders flagged a growing tendency for teams to accept AI-generated analyses without interrogating the underlying logic.
By contrast, the skills sitting in the relatively protecte

Own Your Context, Rent the Intelligence
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/2029590573963935744/XZR-n0C__normal.jpg)](http://x.com/TomSolidPM)
[Thomas Roedl](http://x.com/TomSolidPM)

·
23h
Follow

2
5
43
[5.2K](http://x.com/TomSolidPM/status/2071200096075575302/analytics)
Your notes are in one app. Your tasks are in another. Your thinking is scattered across three or four AI tools that don’t talk to each other. And every time you finally build something that works, the tool gets bought, or shut down, or quietly pivots, and the structure you built walks out the door with it.
If you’ve been at this a while, you’ve already lived the graveyard. Roam Research, Obsidian, Notion, Mem, Tana, Heptabase. I reviewed every one of them on my channel since 2017\. I moved into each one, and every time one died I lost the structure I’d built inside it. The notes exported fine. The thinking did not. If that’s you too, then this is for you.
Here’s what’s new this month, and it’s the part that should make you sit up. Every one of those tools is now offering to remember it all for you. Two days ago Anthropic put Claude inside Slack. You tag it in, you hand it a task, and it goes and does the work while you focus on something else. It’s not a chatbot you message, it’s a teammate you tag by name, it remembers the channels it lives in, and it acts in the background. Three weeks earlier, on June 4th, OpenAI shipped almost the exact same idea from the other side. ChatGPT now builds a memory of you across years of your past conversations and updates the picture on its own. You don’t save anything. It just learns you while you sleep.
It’s genuinely useful, and that’s exactly why it’s a trap. On day one it never feels like one. Day one it’s pure convenience. So here’s what I want to show you: the pattern of why this trap springs about six months later, and the one move that makes you immune to it.
Three things you leave with. One, why this is the whole industry and not one company being evil. Two, which part of all this is actually expensive, and why you’re handing it over for free. Three, the setup I run every day so I never have to care which model wins this month, and it’s fully free.
##
Why they’re all reaching for the same thing
Same month, two different companies, the same move. One puts a teammate in your Slack that remembers everything. The other builds a profile of you that updates while you sleep.
So why are they all doing it at once? Well, it’s not a coincidence and it’s not a conspiracy. It’s incentives. The model is a commodity now. A better one ships every few weeks, so they can’t lock you in with the model anymore. They lock you in with your memory instead. The layer that remembers your decisions, your history, your context. Whoever owns that layer owns you. Andrew Karpathy, probably the most trusted voice in this whole field, called it the third major redesign of how we use AI: first a website you go to, then an app you download, now “a self-contained, persistent entity with your whole organization’s tools and context working alongside your team.” The shift is real. But being excited about the shift and handing over your context are two completely different decisions, and almost nobody is separating them.
##
How the trap actually springs
So how does it close? Well, on day one there is no trap. There’s just a tool that saves you 20 minutes. That’s the whole genius of it.
You tag it once, it pulls the right doc. Helpful. You tag it again, it remembers what your team decided last week. Even more helpful. A month in, it knows your projects, your clients, your shorthand. Thre

🔗 myICOR. AI is the hook. ICOR is the stay.

komet💫 (@jonkomet)

##
To view keyboard shortcuts, press question mark
[View keyboard shortcuts](http://x.com/i/keyboard%5Fshortcuts)
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HLwd60QW4AEoJV8?format=jpg&name=900x900)](http://x.com/jonkomet/article/2071262054518825179/media/2070562824980455425)
The DeepThink Skill: How I Make AI Agents Slow Down Before Expensive Decisions
[![](https://pbs.twimg.com/profile_images/2044107969873276928/Ux-mlU_6_normal.jpg)](http://x.com/jonkomet)
[komet![💫](https://abs.twimg.com/emoji/v2/svg/1f4ab.svg)](http://x.com/jonkomet)
[@jonkomet](http://x.com/jonkomet)
·
14h
Follow
Click to Follow jonkomet
1
18
[1.8K](http://x.com/jonkomet/status/2071262054518825179/analytics)
Most AI agents have one dangerous default:
They move.
That is the whole pitch, right? Give the agent a task, let it call tools, write code, search docs, open files, edit things, test things, and keep going.
Most of the time, that is exactly what you want.
But some tasks should not start with motion. They should start with judgment.
If an agent is about to choose an architecture, rewrite a working system, change pricing, debug a recurring failure, touch security-sensitive code, or commit a public launch direction, the first plausible answer is often the most expensive one.
So I built a Hermes skill called DeepThink.
DeepThink is not a model. It is not a plugin. It is not magic. It is a reusable operating mode that tells an agent:
Slow down. Restate the real decision. Separate facts from guesses. Generate options. Red-team them. Score the tradeoffs. Recommend one path. End with the next safe step.
The point is not longer answers. The point is better judgment.
Why Agents Need A Slow Mode
A good agent should not behave the same way on every task.
Some work is low-risk:
\- rename this file - summarize this doc - fix this obvious typo - run the formatter - find where this function is used
For that kind of work, speed is the feature.
But other work has blast radius:
\- Should we rebuild this service or patch it? - Should we migrate databases before launch? - Should we use one backend or split into separate services? - Is this bug caused by storage, sync, auth, or UI state? - Should this agent get access to production credentials? - Should we automate this workflow or keep a human approval step?
On those tasks, speed can become confidence theater.
The agent sounds sure because language models are good at sounding sure. But underneath the polished answer, it may be mixing verified facts, assumptions, guesses, and vibes.
DeepThink exists for those moments.
It gives the agent a structured way to pause before execution.
##
The Core Rule
DeepThink has one job: Convert vague pressure into a grounded recommendation with evidence, tradeoffs, and the next safe step.
That phrase matters. Not a 4,000-word essay. Not a list of every possible path. Not a philosophical meditation on uncertainty. A grounded recommendation.
The agent should still decide. It should just decide after doing the work.
##
The DeepThink Loop
The workflow is simple:
1\. Restate the real decision. 2\. Identify assumptions. 3\. Separate known facts from unknowns. 4\. Gather evidence if tools are available. 5\. Generate 2 to 4 viable paths. 6\. Red-team each path. 7\. Score impact, risk, reversibility, timing fit, and confidence. 8\. Recommend one path. 9\. End with the next safe step.
The loop idea was partly inspired by \[OpenMythos\](
<https://github.com/kyegomez/OpenMythos>
) and the broader idea of recurrent or looped reasoning: keep bringing the original problem back into the process so the reasoning does not drift.
DeepThink applies that idea at the agent workflow level.
The agent does not just "think harder." It keeps returning to the decision and asking:
\- What do we actually know? - What are we assuming? - What would make this fail? - Which choice is easiest to reverse? - What is the next safe step?
That last question is the whole thing.

item.content:encoded:
Bilgin Ibryam (@bibryam)

🎯How to Write an Effective Software Design Docs

tip: If a decision is easy to change later, it usually does not belong in the design doc.

https://refactoringenglish.com/excerpts/write-an-effective-design-doc/

🔗 How to Write an Effective Software Design Document · Refactoring English

How to Write an Effective Software Design Document
A good design doc can save you years of development time. Writing a design doc forces you to think through important decisions before you waste time on the wrong implementation or paint yourself into a corner. It’s also the best way to coordinate design decisions among teammates and partner teams.
I’ve written design docs as a developer at Google, Microsoft, and within [my own companies](https://mtlynch.io/projects/). The specifics vary, but the underlying principles remain the same. A design doc should articulate the hard problems you’re solving and help your teammates give you feedback.
Below, I share my approach to creating effective design docs and explain what belongs in a design doc and what does not.
- [An example design doc](https://refactoringenglish.com#an-example-design-doc)
- [When should you write a design doc?](https://refactoringenglish.com#when-should-you-write-a-design-doc)
- [How much should you invest into your design doc?](https://refactoringenglish.com#how-much-should-you-invest-into-your-design-doc)
- [What belongs in a design doc?](https://refactoringenglish.com#what-belongs-in-a-design-doc)
- [Components of a design doc](https://refactoringenglish.com#components-of-a-design-doc)
- [Driving Your Design Doc through Review](https://refactoringenglish.com#driving-your-design-doc-through-review)
An example design doc[🔗](https://refactoringenglish.com#an-example-design-doc)
The most common question I get about design docs is where to find a good one. I’ve never seen a public design doc that I consider high-quality. All of mine are hidden away at the companies that paid me to write them.
So, I wrote [a design doc from scratch](https://refactoringenglish.com/little-moments-design-doc/) based on the principles I’m sharing here. It lays out the design for [a real web app I’m building](https://codeberg.org/mtlynch/little-moments).
I created the design doc before writing any code, and I’m adhering to the design [as I implement the app](https://codeberg.org/mtlynch/little-moments#status).
The design is more exhaustive than what I’d normally write for a solo hobby project, but this is roughly the length and depth of a design doc I’d create if I were coordinating work with other people on a professional project.
When should you write a design doc?[🔗](https://refactoringenglish.com#when-should-you-write-a-design-doc)
The more complex or risky the project, the more valuable it is to write a design doc.
Consider these questions:
- Will multiple people coordinate work to implement the design?
- Will the project take more than three months of full-time dev work?
- Will the implementation run in production for several years?
- Does the project involve cross-team collaboration?
- Are the goals and requirements of the project ambiguous?
- Are there catastrophic risks you could prevent at design time (e.g., security flaws, legal risks)?
If you answered “yes” to any of these questions, then it’s likely worth the effort to write a design doc. If you answered “yes” to two or more, a design doc will almost certainly be worth the effort.
How much should you invest into your design doc?[🔗](https://refactoringenglish.com#how-much-should-you-invest-into-your-design-doc)
A design doc can be a simple one-pager or a 50-page document that requires signoff from five different teams. You need to decide how much detail makes sense.
There’s no universal rule that says how long you should spend on a design doc just like there’s no rule that says how much to test your code. The right investment depends on your team’s goals, risks, deadlines, and culture. Sometimes, the right amount to invest in a design doc is zero.
What belongs in a design doc?[🔗](https://refactoringenglish.com#what-belongs-in-a-design-doc)
If you specify every possible detail in a design doc, you’ve essentially written the implementation during the design phase. That would defeat the whole purpose of a design doc.
As a rule o

Tweet: https://x.com/MarcJSchmidt/status/2071368991537279292 Image URLs: - https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL7vwhGX0AAZl2z.png Linked content: - https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL7vwhGX0AAZl2z.png: https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL7vwhGX0AAZl2z.png
item.content:encoded:
Marc (@MarcJSchmidt)

I remember seeing this from @FreyaHolmer for the first time and going "wtf, I got gaslit". I've shown this to many of my programmer friends without math background and most of them were "wait, that's it?". Yes, that's literally it. Obviously only the surface of what math has to offer, but the same principles apply to all sorts of other notations. If you give the (pseudo) code next to it, nice code highlighting, with introspection, definition jumping, debugging, you make Math actually easy to understand and approachable - exactly what we did with programming languages over decades with all these nice tools we now have.
There's a reason some programming languages are more popular than others, but you can do most things with either. And I think the same lens explains math notation: it's not that the concepts are complex, it's that the compression rate is so high that most people bail the fuck out and think this stuff is super complex, when in reality it is not. The underlying principles are super easy once you approach them in a different format (like most of my programmer colleagues here did with approachable languages like JavaScript), it's all about the notation, abstractions, and tools used, and math manages to be the most compact and the most ugly at the same time to me (although I got more used to it over the years).
Programming languages in that same compact category failed hard, for a good reason, people avoid what is unpleasant to look at, read, and requires a big corpus of prerequisites and working memory. I'm actually kind of afraid to think about how many brilliant people avoided math purely because of the notation, not because of the complexity. My theory is that good math people aren't inherently smarter; they just parse and memorize these ugly symbols better or got used to them much earlier in brain development. You can see it clearly in the programming world, where way more people are comfortable writing pretty complicated code but would never touch the most basic math primitives.
It almost feels like math notation is compressed so hard that your brain has to do all the unfolding manually, you hold this huge unpacked state in your head just to work on it, and learning to do that is the hard part most people never push through, so they bail. But code itself has it unfolded for you already: explorable, debuggable, jump-to-definition, back and forth. Your brain doesn't have to hold the whole thing at once, so it can actually chunk it and reason about it much better. The fact that you can modify it and get instant computed feedback in a particular actual real-world use-case makes it much easier to burn an intuition into your brain. Programming runs at a high bandwidth by default, some say too verbose; I say it's an equilibrium evolved over decades, and the proof is the millions of programmers worldwide.

item.content:encoded:
Darryl Ruggles (@RDarrylR)

S3 has been around forever and in recent times, AWS has kept expanding what you can do with it. Recently S3 Files was announced and it has a lot of use cases where it makes sense. One typical pattern with Lambda functions is downloading objects to /tmp, processing them, and uploading the result, plus all the boilerplate for transfers, capacity checks, and cleanup. Amazon S3 Files takes a different angle.

The new approach is mounting an S3 bucket directly as a local file system, so your function just reads and writes at a path like /mnt/data and sync happens behind the scenes. The transfer code disappears and the /tmp size limit stops being a constraint you have to design around.

Sharan Sutrapu shows three real cases including a shared workspace for multi-agent AI, thumbnail generation, and a CSV to Parquet pipeline. Check it out!

# Stop Downloading to `/tmp`: Modernizing AWS Lambda + S3 Workloads with Amazon S3 Files
[![Sharan Sutrapu](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:32:32/1*58xYbbStYLXEiQoUc4-B1A.jpeg)](https://lckhd.eu/@sharansutrapu?source=post%5Fpage---byline--5b9fcca2153c---------------------------------------)

![](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fit:700/1*n2-qnDRD744bVrmqOVRrcQ.jpeg)
_Simplify your serverless architectures by mounting S3 directly as a local file system._
AWS Lambda functions that interact with Amazon S3 typically follow a very familiar pattern: download an object to local ephemeral storage (`/tmp`), process it locally, and upload the result back to S3\. While reliable, this well-understood approach forces developers to write boilerplate code for managing transfers, monitoring `/tmp` capacity, and cleaning up storage, all of which distracts from your actual processing logic.
Enter **Amazon S3 Files**.
S3 Files revolutionizes this workflow by allowing your Lambda function to mount an S3 bucket directly as a local file system. Your function reads and writes files at a local mount path (e.g., `/mnt/data`), and the file system handles synchronization with S3 automatically behind the scenes. The result? The transfer code disappears, the `/tmp` size constraints vanish, and your developer experience drastically improves.
Let’s walk through three common Lambda + S3 workloads to see how S3 Files modernizes each one.
## Getting Started
To integrate a Lambda function with S3 Files, you only need three steps:
1. **Create an S3 file system:** Do this via the S3 console, AWS CLI, or CloudFormation. This single operation creates the file system, mount targets in your VPC, and an access point.
2. **Configure your Lambda function:** Specify the access point ARN and a local mount path (e.g., `/mnt/data`). Ensure your function is in a VPC with access to the mount target and has at least 512 MB of memory to enable direct

The American A.I. chaos of recent weeks is profoundly self-defeating. With its actions against Anthropic, the U.S. government is skating close to its own Jack Ma moment.

We often think of A.I. as a race between the United States and China. Instead we are seeing the emergence of an even more acute form of competition, between the public power of governments and the private power of ambitious companies.

The challenges of regulating A.I. at the frontier are urgent and important. The U.S. government needs to strike a better balance between ambition and control, lest it irrevocably damage America’s long-term technological edge.

item.content:encoded:
arshad (@arshadyaseeen)

I wrote this article to describe the design discipline I used to build Yuku.

https://arshad.fyi/writings/engineering-high-performance-parsers https://t.co/1O9EZKDFam

🔗 Engineering High-Performance Parsers with Data-Oriented Design - Arshad Yaseen

Engineering High-Performance Parsers with Data-Oriented Design
[Abstract](https://www.arshad.fyi#abstract)
A parser is usually taught as a problem of grammars, but once the grammar is correct, almost all of the performance and most of the engineering difficulty live somewhere else, in how the resulting tree is represented in memory. This article describes the design discipline I used to build [Yuku](https://yuku.fyi), a JavaScript and TypeScript parser written in Zig that runs several times faster than the established parsers in its category, and it applies to any parser or compiler frontend in a native language. The claim is simple. Design the data structure first, let the machine’s access patterns dictate its shape, and the speed follows almost for free, while unrelated-looking problems (memory layout, allocation, and serialization) collapse into one solution.
[1. The Single Idea](https://www.arshad.fyi#1-the-single-idea)
A parser’s performance is decided long before its first benchmark, by how its tree is laid out in memory. That is data-oriented design. Start from the access pattern and the hardware, derive the representation, and build everything else, the lexer, the recursive descent, the visitor API, to serve it.
Two facts about modern hardware drive the whole argument.
- A cache miss to main memory costs on the order of a hundred nanoseconds. A floating-point operation costs a fraction of one. A parser that chases pointers is memory-latency-bound, stalling on loads rather than computing.
- A general-purpose allocator call is not free, and a parser that allocates one node at a time pays that cost millions of times while scattering related objects across memory.
The stakes are concrete. A hundred-thousand-byte file produces roughly fifty thousand AST nodes. As separately allocated, pointer-linked objects, that is fifty thousand allocations, as many frees, and every later traversal chasing pointers into cold memory. In one flat array, it is a handful of allocations, a linear scan, and a single teardown. That is not a constant factor. It changes the slope of the curve.
[2. The Cost of the Obvious Design](https://www.arshad.fyi#2-the-cost-of-the-obvious-design)
The textbook AST is a tree of heap-allocated structs joined by pointers. In a native language it looks like this.
const Node = union(enum) {
binary: struct { op: Op, left: *Node, right: *Node },
call: struct { callee: *Node, args: []*Node },
identifier: struct { name: []const u8 },
// ...one variant per node kind
};It is correct, it is readable, and it is the wrong shape for a machine. Consider what it costs.
- Allocation per node. Each *Nodeis an allocator call. For our hundred-thousand-byte file that is tens of thousands of calls, each touching allocator metadata.
- Pointer chasing. leftandrightpoint wherever the allocator happened to place them. Walking the tree is a sequence of unpredictable loads, each a potential cache miss. The prefetcher cannot help because the addresses are not a pattern.
- Pointer overhead. On a 64-bit target every edge is eight bytes. A node with two children spends sixteen bytes just on pointers, often more than its actual payload. Pointers also pin the representation to one address space, which makes the tree impossible to hand to another language without a deep copy.
- Fragmentation and teardown. Freeing the tree is another tens of thousands of calls, and the objects were never contiguous to begin with.
The variant payloads also differ wildly in size, so a naive node array would be sized to the largest variant and waste space on the common small ones. We will fix that too.
None of these costs come from the grammar. They come from the representation. So we change the representation.
[3. Nodes as Indices, Not Pointers](https://www.arshad.fyi#3-nodes-as-indices-not-pointers)
The first move is to replace every pointer with an integer index into one flat array of nodes.
pub const NodeIndex = enum(u32) {
null = std.math.ma

item.content:encoded:
Voltex (@VoltexGar)

Boris Cherny, Head of Claude Code, Anthropic:

"you can define a stop hook that's like, if the tests don't pass, keep going. essentially it's like you can just make the model keep going until the thing is done."

that one config is the post's loop #1, straight from the person who built the tool. a stop hook fires every time the turn ends, so the work can't be called done until tests and lint go green. deterministic, zero effort, the loop most people skip.

cherny describes the verification loop in his own words too: for big changes his team spawns subagents to find every issue, one checking claude.md compliance, one combing git history, one hunting bugs, then five more subagents whose only job is to kill the false positives. a fresh clean-context critic catches what the builder talked itself past.

and the memory loop, in his words: if you see a mistake, you just tell claude to add it to claude.md, so next time it already knows. the correction outlives the session it happened in.

four loops, none exotic. each is a few lines of config or one instruction. seniors out-ship everyone else because they run all four at once, not because their model is smarter.

##
What is Hermes, and how is it different from Claude Code?
[Hermes Agent](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/)
is an open-source agent runtime from
[Nous Research](https://nousresearch.com/)
. It can run on your machine or on a remote server. It can use tools, load skills, keep memory across sessions, run scheduled work, spawn subagents, and talk to you through a CLI, desktop app, Telegram, Discord, or dashboard.
[Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/overview)
is best for a focused work session. You point it at a repo and ask it to inspect files, change code, run checks, explain the diff, and stop. The center of gravity is the codebase and the current session.
Hermes aims at longer-lived agent work. Its center of gravity is the agent environment: memory, sessions, skills, gateways, scheduled jobs, and surfaces you can reach later.
The practical split:
* Use Claude Code when the task is a bounded coding session.
* Consider Hermes when the task needs memory, repeat work, messaging access, or long-lived state.
So the choice depends on the job.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL5AMd7agAATDzV?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/nurijanian/article/2071164077377032237/media/2071163461573443584)
##
How is Hermes different from OpenClaw?
[Akshay Pachaar’s Hermes masterclass](https://x.com/akshay%5Fpachaar/status/2054564519280804028)
frames the difference this way:
> Hermes packages a gateway around a learning agent. OpenClaw packages an agent around a messaging gateway.
Both tools live in the same broad category: persistent agents, messaging surfaces, skills, tools, memory, and remote use. The difference is what each system seems to treat as the center.
[OpenClaw](https://docs.openclaw.ai/)
is more messaging-gateway-first. It is strong when you want an agent reachable through chat-like channels and workflows around that gateway.
Hermes is more learning-agent-first. Its pitch is that the agent gets better from use. It keeps bounded memory, searches past sessions, writes or updates skills, runs background review passes, and can use scheduled jobs or subagents inside the same environment.
The masterclass describes Hermes as combining three things that usually sit apart:
* runtime skill learning
* persistent multi-layer memory
* optional offline skill improvement through
[GEPA](https://github.com/NousResearch/hermes-agent-self-evolution/)
For a PM, the practical reading is simple:
If the main job is “I want to message an agent from different places,” OpenClaw is the adjacent reference point. If the main job is “I want an agent that remembers, builds skills from repeated work, and can run as a broader personal agent environment,” Hermes is the system to study.
[![Image](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HL5AOaSa8AAfIIm?format=jpg&name=small)](http://x.com/nurijanian/article/2071164077377032237/media/2071163494955937792)
##
Three real use cases people have said Hermes is good at
1\. Source collection and research workflows
The strongest PM-relevant example is
[Artem Zhutov’s Hermes plus Obsidian workflow](https://artemxtech.substack.com/p/i-stopp

item.content:encoded:
Anastasiia Gaidashenko (@avgaydashenko)

good LW post on productivity techniques (link below)
went through it and checked what I actually do vs. what didn't stick

works for me
- task capture: I log every ~15-30min of work hours in my calendar and have AI generate an end-of-day summary
- underschedule: a deliberate weekly block of unplanned time (tho I got here through hypercontrol work, not productivity literature)
- focus on the wildly important: "only hell yes" rule (will write a separate post on my prioritization framework at some point...)
- rest / solitude / productive meditation: honestly my favorite category haha (jacuzzi, weighted blanket, sensory walks, breathwork, jazz clubs, baths, etc etc...)
- also: CBT and EMDR, coaching calls, strength + mobility + endurance 3x+/week, and working with a human personal assistant (not AI!)

didn't stick
- app blockers (SelfControl, Freedom)
- spaced repetition software (tried but abandoned)

the thing the post almost gets to but doesn't quite say: the post ends with "don't make yourself crazy" and flags that rigid scheduling fails where flexible planning survives
what I learned through hypercontrol work is that the urge to systematize everything can be anxiety in disguise rather than genuine productivity
so I spent quite a few years identifying which control patterns were net positive and keeping only those...

http://lesswrong.com/posts/P3zrurj5hHKFKDL3M/productivity-working-towards-a-summary-of-what-we-know

🔗 Productivity: Working towards a summary of what we know — LessWrong

[Epistemic effort](https://www.lesswrong.com/lw/o6m/epistemic_effort)
- Spent 20-30 hours researching what we know about productivity. About an hour a day for two weeks, plus a few more days where I dedicated more than an hour to studying productivity.
- Skimmed through the entire [archives](http://calnewport.com/blog/archive/)of Cal Newport's blog (the author of[Deep Work,](http://calnewport.com/books/deep-work/)which I had read about a year or two ago), and read the posts that seem most useful.
- Searched through lesswrong.com and lesserwrong.com and read relevant and useful posts, including [How to Beat Procrastination](https://www.lesswrong.com/lw/3w3/how_to_beat_procrastination).
- Searched Google and Google Scholar for academic research on productivity (I couldn't really find anything).
- Read a few Harvard Business Review articles on productivity, starting with [For Real Productivity, Less is Truly More](https://hbr.org/2010/05/for-real-productivity-less-is).
- Read a few [summaries](https://blog.zenkit.com/a-beginners-guide-to-getting-things-done-3cc1a5123b98)of[Getting Things Done](http://gettingthingsdone.com/), by David Allen. Watched his[Ted Talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CHxhjDPKfbY).
- Read through about 5-7 pages of the highest voted questions on the [Personal Productivity Stack Exchange](https://productivity.stackexchange.com/questions)and went down some[link rabbit holes](https://xkcd.com/214/).
- Spent about two hours thinking about how to categorize productivity advice.
- I have a degree in neuroscience, know a decent amount about cognitive sciences more generally, and have read various related books such as [Peak](https://www.amazon.com/Peak-Secrets-New-Science-Expertise/dp/1531864880)by Anders Ericsson, which reviews what we know about expert performance.
- Spent about 20 hours writing and editing this post.
Meta
I've come across a lot of productivity-related advice over the years. Tips, tricks, blog posts, books, etc. I feel like I know a decent amount about productivity, and that I should be pretty damn productive. Unfortunately, the knowledge I've accumulated doesn't seem to have translated into actual success. Actual productivity.
So then, a few weeks ago I decided that enough is enough. That I need to take a step back and really spend some time "getting better at productivity". In order to "get better at productivity", I figured that I should [start off](https://www.lesswrong.com/lw/3m3/the_neglected_virtue_of_scholarship) doing some research. Why try to figure things out myself when I could just start off standing on the shoulders of others? This post outlines and summarizes what I have found in my research.
I initially wasn't planning on writing this post. I don't study productivity professionally. I'm not the most qualified person to be doing this. I've only spent 20-30 hours researching this, so there must be a lot of things I'm missing. Still, I think that there are some strong reasons for writing this post:
- I couldn't find a similar post that already exists. Maybe that's just because I'm a bad googler. Maybe it's because they're actually hard to find. Maybe it's because they don't exist in the first place. I'm not sure which of these are true, but I suspect that the last two are true to a notable degree. If not, I apologize for adding to the pile of shitty articles on the internet.
- My writing style may make things "click" for certain readers. Scott Alexander just wrote a cool article about this idea: [Non-Expert Explanation](http://slatestarcodex.com/2017/11/02/non-expert-explanation/).
- Hopefully commenters will add new information. I am attempting to summarize what is known (and thought) about productivity, but since I'm not an expert in this field, I expect that my attempt at summarizing will be incomplete and imperfect. I intend for this post to be a starting point. I hope that readers will share their knowledge, and perhaps we as a community can create a pretty awesome outline a

item.content:encoded:
h100envy (@h100envy)

This paper completely changed how I think about assembling a RAG pipeline:

Define the nodes -> List candidates for each -> Run them on your dataset -> Keep the winner -> Move to the next node

Here is the 5-step blueprint:

Nodes: the pipeline is split into stages - query expansion, retrieval, augmenter, reranker, prompt maker.

Candidates: each node gets a set of interchangeable modules - BM25, vectordb, hybrids, rerankers.

Greedy per node: you optimize nodes one at a time, locking the best module before moving on.

Two metrics: retrieval is measured separately from generation, so you see exactly where quality leaks.

On your own data: the optimum is searched on your corpus, not a foreign leaderboard - the best module for Wikipedia QA fails on domain docs.

Key insight: the best RAG pipeline is not picked from a benchmark, it is found by search on your own dataset.

Five pipeline stages, each with a pool of interchangeable modules, and the loop assembles the winning combination on its own.
